title: Boolean Algebra and Logic Circuits
overview: A2 logic moves beyond basic gates to adders, flip-flops, Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps. You need to derive truth tables/circuits, understand one-bit storage, simplify expressions correctly and minimise circuits using K-maps.
syllabusPoints: Construct/use truth tables for half adders and full adders.
Explain SR and JK flip-flops as data-storage elements.
Apply Boolean laws including De Morgan's laws to simplify expressions.
Use Karnaugh maps to derive simplified Boolean expressions and explain their benefit.

definitions.definition: Adds two input bits and outputs Sum and Carry.
Adds two bits plus CarryIn and outputs Sum and CarryOut.
A bistable sequential circuit capable of storing one bit of state.
A visual map of truth-table outputs used to group adjacent values and minimise Boolean expressions.
Rules that distribute NOT over AND/OR while swapping the operator.

sections.title: Half and full adders
content: For a half adder, Sum is A XOR B and Carry is A AND B. A full adder includes CarryIn so units can be chained to add multi-bit binary values.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Half adder: S = A XOR B; C = A AND B

sections.title: SR and JK flip-flops
content: An SR flip-flop has Set/Reset control and stores output Q. A basic SR design has a forbidden/ambiguous input combination. The JK design resolves that case: when J=K=1 the output toggles. Flip-flops are building blocks for registers/counters/state memory.

sections.title: Boolean algebra
content: Use identity, complement, absorption, idempotent and distributive laws plus De Morgan. A simplification is valid only if it preserves the truth table.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
NOT(A.B) = NOT A + NOT B
NOT(A+B) = NOT A . NOT B

sections.title: Karnaugh maps
content: Place outputs in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ by one variable. Group adjacent 1s in rectangles of size 1,2,4,8...; make groups as large as possible and allow wrap-around adjacency. Variables that change inside a group disappear from the simplified term.

sections.title: Why simplify
content: Fewer terms/gates can reduce hardware cost, propagation delay, power use and opportunities for error. K-maps give a systematic visual way to find such reductions for small variable counts.

examTips: K-map groups must be powers of two and horizontal/vertical, not diagonal.
Use Gray-code ordering and remember opposite edges can be adjacent.
For adders, distinguish CarryIn from CarryOut.
commonMistakes: Using ordinary binary order on K-map axes.
Forgetting CarryIn on a full adder.
Treating a flip-flop as combinational logic with no state.
quickRecall: De Morgan swaps AND/OR under NOT
